paras: The Chicago manhunt for Zeph Davis was a crowd search of a Chicago neighborhood near the Desplaines street police station on the afternoon of February 28, 1888, in which two Black boys mistaken for Davis, a man accused of murder, were nearly killed. According to the New York Sun, some 5,000 men and boys joined the police, ransacked houses and drove the Black residents into the streets until news of Davis's capture outside the city ended the hunt.

Davis, described as a "mulatto," was accused of killing Maggie Gaughan with a hatchet in a boot-heel factory on State street and of fleeing the city by freight train. The Chicago police sent his description to the railroads, and a constable named Martin arrested him near Forest, Illinois, where Davis confessed to the killing but denied assaulting the girl. At Forest, farmers who had been "clamoring to lynch him" rushed at the prisoner, and one lunged at him with a knife through the train window.

In Chicago, before word of the arrest arrived, policeman John Wheeler of the Desplaines street station thought he saw Davis run from Union street into Meridian street and sent in an alarm. Police then searched the block bounded by Madison, Meridian, Union and Desplaines streets; the Sun counted fifteen officers, while the Illinois Staats-Zeitung said the whole reserve of the nearby station took part. The Sun reported that the news drew 5,000 men and boys, who overturned beds, barrels and boxes in the "tumble-down dens" and drove "the colored inmates of the houses" into the streets.

In the same account, two Black boys "who bore a striking resemblance to the murderer, were nearly killed before they could prove their identity." The hunt lasted until about 2 o'clock, when confirmation of the capture at Forest dispersed the crowd.

Davis was brought back that evening and taken off the train at the Twenty-second street station rather than the Polk street depot, where, the Sun said, "an immense crowd" was waiting and he "would have been lynched in short order." No report of arrests, injuries treated or any official inquiry into the attack on the two boys appears in the coverage.

The Sun's Chicago dispatch placed the hunt in its final paragraph, beneath the subhead "An Exciting Hunt in the City," and reported the attack on the boys without comment. The German-language Illinois Staats-Zeitung of Chicago headlined Davis as "das schwarze Scheusal" (the black monster) and also called its account of the search "an exciting hunt." Its version followed a single fleeing Black man who was never found, and remarked that he was lucky, since the excited crowd might have taken him for Davis and hanged him from the nearest lamppost.
Other papers, such as the Washington Evening Star, printed Davis's confession but did not mention the Chicago crowd.

Only the Sun reports that Black residents were driven out and that two boys were nearly killed, and only it gives a crowd size of 5,000. The local Staats-Zeitung describes the same search and crowd but mentions no one harmed, so the attack on the boys rests on the Sun's dispatch alone.

reader.title: Chicago manhunt for Zeph Davis
bases: A crowd hunting an accused murderer ransacked Black homes, drove the residents into the streets and nearly killed two Black boys who resembled him; no one was reported killed (A1, A4).

The manhunt and the excited crowd in the Desplaines and Madison street district are reported independently by the Sun and the Illinois Staats-Zeitung (A1, A4), but the attack on the two Black boys and the eviction of Black residents appear only in the Sun's dispatch (A1).

accounts.label: Sun's Chicago dispatch
accounts.gist: After Wheeler's alarm, fifteen policemen and 5,000 men and boys searched the block, overturned furnishings, drove the Black residents into the streets and nearly killed two Black boys who resembled Davis; news of the capture dispersed the mob about 2 o'clock.

accounts.label: Illinois Staats-Zeitung (Chicago)
accounts.gist: Two policemen chased a Black man who matched Davis's description into a house on Meridian street; police searched house to house without finding him, and the paper said the excited crowd might have hanged him from a lamppost had he been caught; the excitement ended with news of the capture.

framing.detail: The Sun ran the hunt as the last paragraph of 'MAGGIE GAUGHAN'S SLAYER CAUGHT' under the subhead 'An Exciting Hunt in the City,' reporting the attack on the boys without comment.

The Staats-Zeitung headlined Davis as 'Das schwarze Scheusal' and 'Der schwarze Teufel', and said the man chased 'could count himself lucky' that the crowd did not take him for Davis and string him up.

conflicts.note: The accounts do not directly contradict each other, but only the Sun reports violence; the Staats-Zeitung is the local paper and mentions no injuries.
